Unlike search-based repair methods that require a linear scan of the network to select the repair plan, the certificate selectors introduced here operate in $O(1)$ time and $O(1)$ memory, consulting only the fault coordinates. This paper develops this stronger formulation for the one- and two-fault regime: a constant-time certificate selector. Given only the faulty coordinates, the selector classifies the relative fault geometry, chooses a coordinate-reduction orientation, and returns a bounded ordered set of component-crossing repair edges. For dense Gaussian networks $G_k$, every source-free fault set with $|F|\le2$ is repaired with depth at most $k+2$ and with exactly $c-1$ external component-crossing edges for the selected fault-pruned orientation. For dense EJ networks $H_t$, every one-fault placement is repaired within depth $t+1$, and every two-fault placement is repaired within depth $t+2$, again with exactly $c-1$ external repair edges. Exhaustive strict validation confirms the Gaussian selector over $146{,}156$ one- and two-fault cases for $k=5,\ldots,12$ and the EJ selector over $52{,}395$ cases for $t=2,\ldots,8$, with zero failures in connectivity, acyclicity, exact repair count, or depth bound.

</details>


### [354] [Re-Rooting-Assisted Edge-Minimum Runtime Repair for Node and Link Failures in Dense Eisenstein--Jacobi Broadcast Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21133)
*Bader Albader*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents a method for broadcasting in dense EJ networks that recovers effectively from node/link failures by analyzing specific tree structures and connectivity conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for robust broadcasting methods in dense EJ networks due to the fragility of diameter-level spanning trees under node/link failures.

Method: The paper introduces a selected triple $(r,θ,	ext{Kcomp}_{r,θ})$ to analyze the fault recovery process and provides a necessary and sufficient condition for successful repairs based on graph connectivity.

Result: The study shows that recovery is ensured if the induced healthy graph $G'$ is connected, leading to successful spanning tree mappings and guaranteed recovery under specific conditions.

Conclusion: The approach was validated through extensive trials, achieving 100% recovery and demonstrating efficiency improvements in repair edges over traditional methods.

Abstract: One-to-all broadcasting in dense Eisenstein--Jacobi (EJ) networks relies on diameter-level spanning trees that fragment when nodes or links fail. This paper introduces the selected triple $(r,θ,\Kcomp_{r,θ})$--a chosen root, a chosen EJ coordinate-reduction orientation, and the healthy component graph induced by that choice--as the fundamental unit of analysis for joint node/link fault recovery. The central result is a necessary and sufficient condition: hybrid repair succeeds if and only if the healthy EJ graph $G'=\Ht-\Fv-\Fe$ is connected. When $G'$ is connected, a spanning tree of $\Kcomp_{r,θ}$ maps to exactly $c-1$ component-crossing repair edges, which is minimum for the selected pruned tree. Deterministic guarantees include: one/two faulty nodes are always placed on the distance-$t$ boundary by re-rooting; a single failed link is either avoided or repaired by exactly one crossing edge; and the repaired depth satisfies $D_{r,θ}\le 2t+1$ under shallowest-layer entry selection. A 260,000-trial validation campaign confirms 100\% recovery and substantial repair-edge reduction over fixed-source repair across five network scales up to $N=120601$ nodes, while global-BFS, near-miss, and cap-sensitivity audits clarify the tradeoff between reachability, forwarding-state changes, and ranked root selection.

</details>


### [355] [Re-Rooting-Assisted Edge-Minimum Runtime Repair for Node and Link Failures in Dense Gaussian Broadcast Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21134)
*Bader Albader*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper develops a runtime recovery framework for dense Gaussian networks to efficiently handle node and link faults during broadcast operations, demonstrating significant improvements in repair edge reduction and reliability through re-rooting methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the fragility of dense Gaussian networks' broadcast trees under various faults, improving fault tolerance and recovery efficiency.

Method: The framework implements a re-rooting strategy for identifying and managing faults in the network, employing deterministic single-link repairs and boundary intersection techniques for source selection.

Result: Empirical results demonstrate high recovery rates, achieving 100% in deterministic scenarios and approximately 99.998% in multi-link faults, alongside an 80-100% reduction in average repair edges with re-rooting.

Conclusion: The study emphasizes that edge-minimum repair is achievable in dense Gaussian networks, moving away from a focus on universal completion time during recovery.

Abstract: Dense Gaussian networks are degree-four algebraic networks with compact diameter and coordinate-based routing. Their diameter-level broadcast trees are efficient but fragile under node, link, and runtime-discovered faults. This paper develops a runtime recovery framework for dense Gaussian broadcast networks under static node/link faults and mixed faults, plus single-link faults discovered live. The method re-roots the source so known node faults become boundary leaves whenever possible, then filters failed links and repairs gaps by connecting healthy components of the pruned tree. For a selected root with connected healthy component graph, we prove exactly $c-1$ external repair edges are necessary and sufficient. We also prove deterministic single-link repair, give a constant-size boundary-intersection primitive for source selection, derive a link-avoidance exclusion test, and add a local-obstruction bound explaining why high-order cuts vanish as $k$ grows. Experiments over $k\in\{10,25,50,100,200\}$, up to $80{,}401$ nodes, $280{,}000$ static trials, and $15{,}000$ transient trials show 100\% recovery for deterministic and bounded regimes, $99.998\%$ for multi-link faults, and $99.963\%$ for heuristic regimes; non-recovered trials are explained by disconnected components or relocation failure. Re-rooting reduces average repair edges by 80--100\% versus fixed-source repair. Patched Gaussian-link Noxim replays confirm packet-complete execution and show re-rooting reduces repair edges, components, and depth. A completion-cycle audit separates repair benefit from latency: ablations confirm completion time depends on relocation, scheduling, delivery tail, and selector objective, so the paper claims edge-minimum repair rather than universal completion-cycle dominance.

</details>


### [356] [KineticSim: A Lightweight, High-Performance Execution Engine for Real-Time Market Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21784)
*Shakya Jayakody,Prarthinie Jayakody*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents a reusable parallel design pattern for simulating financial markets using GPU frameworks, enhancing efficiency and speed in agent-based simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of traditional CPU simulators and inefficient GPU frameworks in simulating financial markets for applications like market design and stress testing.

Method: The authors introduce a parallel design pattern called persistent, state-carrying clearing, which utilizes shared memory for caching mutable state and enables cooperative clearing of agent actions to improve performance.

Result: The implementation in KineticSim achieves a peak throughput of over 54.7 billion agent-events per second, with significant speedups compared to CPU and other GPU frameworks, while maintaining low memory usage and accurate results.

Conclusion: The proposed pattern not only enhances performance for financial market simulations but is also applicable to other iterative multi-agent tasks requiring state persistence.

Abstract: Simulating financial markets at scale with multi-agent (Agent-Based) models is critical for market design, regulatory stress-testing, and reinforcement learning, but traditional CPU simulators are bottlenecked by sequential processing while vectorized GPU frameworks suffer from kernel-launch overhead and redundant global-memory round-trips. We formalize, analyze, and evaluate a reusable parallel design pattern: persistent, state-carrying clearing for iterative multi-agent reductions. By caching mutable simulation state in thread-block shared memory across step boundaries, aggregating agent actions via shared-memory atomics, and resolving the clearing function cooperatively, the pattern reduces the per-step critical-path depth from Theta(L+A) for sequential clearing (L price-grid ticks, A agents) to Theta(log L + ceil(A/L)) and makes global-memory traffic independent of the step count. We implement this in KineticSim, a lightweight GPU execution engine that simulates massive ensembles of limit-order books in parallel, reaching a peak throughput of over 54.7 billion agent-events per second. On a fixed workload it delivers speedups of 3406x over CPU (NumPy), 27.8x over PyTorch GPU, 42.8x over JAX GPU, and 8.4x over a naive custom CUDA baseline, while using roughly an order of magnitude less GPU memory than PyTorch. Across 53 configurations the two custom CUDA engines produce bitwise-identical order books, and aggregate statistics match the CPU reference to within 0.1%. The pattern generalizes to other iterative multi-agent workloads requiring state-persistent, block-localized reductions.

</details>


### [357] [Recency/Frequency Adaptive KV Caching for Large Language Model Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21238)
*Yang Shen,Meghana Madhyastha,Robert Underwood,Bogdan Nicolae,Randal Burns*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper proposes an adaptive caching technique for key-value caching in large language model inference that improves performance metrics significantly compared to existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The existing least-recently-used (LRU) cache management strategy is insufficient for diverse inference workloads, leading to ineffective cache utilization and interference among unrelated workloads.

Method: The method involves integrating adaptive caching that dynamically allocates cache space between recently accessed and frequently occurring key-value blocks, counteracting the drawbacks of LRU.

Result: The proposed system achieves a cache hit rate improvement of up to 10.8% and reduces time to first token by up to 12.6% for synthetic workloads, with similar but smaller improvements in real-world scenarios.

Conclusion: The adaptive caching method generalizes effectively to batch inference and maintains interpretability while catering to a variety of inference workloads.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a powerful technique for accelerating large language model inference and generation. Inference workloads are large and diverse, which makes them difficult to cache effectively. Existing cache management strategies adopt the least-recently-used policy for evicting cache blocks. However, LRU leads to multiple unrelated workloads flushing each other's caches. To address this, we integrate adaptive caching that dynamically allocates cache space between recently and frequently occurring KV blocks. Evaluations show that it improves the KV cache hit rate by up to 10.8% and reduces time to first token by up to 12.6% over naive vLLM on synthetic document question answering workloads, and 2.1% and 2.0% respectively on real-world conversation workloads. The method generalizes well to batch inference and demonstrates clear interpretability while effectively accommodating diverse workloads.

</details>


### [358] [SwarmX: Agentic Scheduling for Low-Latency Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21401)
*Yeqi Huang,Yanwei Ye,Guomin Chen,Wenhao Su,Bin Gong,Jialian Li,Zhan Lu,Yangshen Deng,Xuan Sun,Le Xu,Luo Mai*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: SwarmX is a novel scheduling system designed for low-latency agentic AI applications in GPU-CPU clusters, addressing scheduling challenges through the use of neural predictors and a scheduler-agent framework, demonstrating significant reductions in tail latency and improved throughput in evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for effective scheduling in agentic AI applications due to their complex model-call structures and dependency on prompt semantics that make traditional scheduling inadequate for low-latency requirements.

Method: SwarmX employs scheduling-specific neural predictors to analyze and predict performance based on various features; integrates these predictors within a scheduler-agent framework for dynamic decision-making and online adaptation.

Result: SwarmX achieves up to 61.5% reduction in tail latency and up to 2x the throughput compared to existing state-of-the-art schedulers during evaluations on extensive production and controlled environments.

Conclusion: The integration and effectiveness of SwarmX in real-world scenarios validate its capability to enhance scheduling for low-latency agentic AI applications.

Abstract: Agentic AI applications compose multiple model calls and tool executions, creating new scheduling challenges for GPU-CPU clusters. Their inference time and model-call structure often depend on prompt semantics, making conventional scheduling approaches ineffective for low-latency serving. This paper presents SwarmX, a system that implements agentic scheduling for low-latency agentic applications. SwarmX uses scheduling-specific neural predictors to capture prompt, device, runtime, and target-model features; exposes distributional predictions to routers and scalers for tail-aware decisions; and provides mechanisms for predictor training and online adaptation. These predictors and mechanisms are integrated into a scheduler-agent framework that provides a common substrate for integration with existing scheduling and model-serving infrastructure. We evaluate SwarmX using production deployment (nearly one thousand GPUs and one million CPU cores) and controlled experiments on a 128-GPU testbed. Across multi-agent code generation, deep research, and multimodal agentic workflows, SwarmX reduces tail latency by up to 61.5% compared to state-of-the-art schedulers and sustains up to 2x the throughput of production schedulers under the same SLO.

</details>


### [359] [Bridging Design and Execution: A Visual Graph Editor for Edge and Cloud Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21416)
*Katarina-Glorija Grujić,Nikola Stanković,Maja Vukasović,Miloš Simić*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper introduces a domain-specific visual graph editor for modeling modular applications in edge and cloud computing, focusing on a unified interface that enhances coordination of computational kernels, shared data, and event-driven execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To facilitate the design and modeling of modular applications in edge and cloud environments, addressing challenges related to data sharing, execution order, and dependencies.

Method: A visual graph editor supporting models with kernels, shared memory nodes, and event triggers, allowing users to create graphs and define data/control flow, which are serialized to machine-readable formats for execution.

Result: The editor improves the reasoning about application components compared to traditional tools by providing modularity, explicit execution semantics, and direct deployability, demonstrated through a federated learning workflow example.

Conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for visual orchestration of modular computation in distributed environments and offers extensibility for user-defined elements, paving the way for exploring complex distributed applications.

Abstract: Designing modular applications for edge and cloud computing environments involves coordinating multiple computational kernels, shared data, and event-driven execution. This paper presents a domain-specific visual graph editor that enables users to model such applications using a unified interface. The editor supports three first-class abstractions: kernels, representing computational units; shared memory nodes, modeling distributed data; and event triggers, capturing execution dependencies. Users can construct graphs visually, configure node properties, and connect elements to define data and control flow. The resulting graphs are automatically serialized into machine-readable representations (JSON/XML) and can be passed to an execution API, bridging the gap between design-time modeling and runtime deployment. The editor's graph-based model improves reasoning about data sharing, execution order, and dependencies, particularly in distributed edge and cloud scenarios. To demonstrate its applicability, we discuss a federated learning workflow, where local training kernels interact with a shared global model through event-driven coordination. Compared to traditional workflow editors and general-purpose diagramming tools, the proposed system provides explicit execution semantics, modularity, and direct deployability. This work lays the foundation for visual orchestration of modular computation in distributed environments and offers extensibility for user-defined kernels, event types, and alternative execution backends, enabling future exploration of complex distributed applications.

</details>


### [360] [rush: Scalable Asynchronous Distributed Computing via Shared State in R](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21430)
*Marc Becker,Bernd Bischl*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: rush is an R package that enables asynchronous parallelization of iterative algorithms using a shared-state model, leveraging Redis for task management and error handling, and it integrates with the mlr3 ecosystem for enhanced optimization workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of asynchronous parallel computing support in R, especially for hyperparameter optimization, contrasting with existing Python frameworks that utilize decentralized approaches.

Method: rush employs a Redis database to provide a shared key-value store for task data, allowing workers to execute tasks asynchronously while managing their lifecycle with a high-level API.

Result: The implementation of rush demonstrated efficient asynchronous decentralized Bayesian optimization (ADBO) in hyperparameter optimization of LightGBM, utilizing 448 workers across four datasets.

Conclusion: rush significantly enhances parallel computing capabilities in R by facilitating decentralized asynchronous task execution, thus bridging a gap in existing R packages for hyperparameter optimization.

Abstract: Many algorithms in statistics and machine learning can be parallelized in an asynchronous manner where workers need to communicate through shared state rather than execute independent tasks dispatched by a central controller. Especially in modern hyperparameter optimization and parallel black-box optimization with expensive objectives, this decentralized approach has become widespread, and several Python frameworks adopt it (e.g., Optuna, DeepHyper, and Hyperopt). However, all popular R packages for parallel computing follow a centralized controller-worker architecture that does not support this pattern. We present rush, an R package that provides a shared-state coordination layer for asynchronously parallelized iterative algorithms. rush uses a Redis database as a shared key-value store: workers read and write task data through the database and independently execute their own loops. The package provides a high-level API for managing tasks and their lifecycle, featuring sub-millisecond per-task overhead, robust error handling with automatic detection of lost workers, and efficient caching. rush optionally integrates with the mlr3 ecosystem, powering asynchronous optimization in the bbotk and mlr3tuning packages. We demonstrate the practical utility of rush by implementing asynchronous decentralized Bayesian optimization (ADBO) and benchmarking it on hyperparameter optimization of LightGBM across four datasets using 448 workers.

</details>


### [361] [Towards Global Multi-Cloud Strategies: Insights into AWS and Alibaba Cloud Synergy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21680)
*Martin G. Zizler,Malte Prieß,Christoph P. Neumann*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: A comparative analysis of AWS and Alibaba Cloud highlights challenges and best practices for IoT workload migration in multi-cloud strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address interoperability and migration issues faced by enterprises adopting multi-cloud strategies.

Method: Comparative analysis of AWS and Alibaba Cloud, focusing on architectural, service, and policy differences, using provider-native and open source Infrastructure-as-Code tools.

Result: Key technical trade-offs and best practices for secure multi-cloud deployments were identified through a case study of IoT workload migration.

Conclusion: The findings provide valuable guidance for organizations seeking to achieve interoperability between AWS and Alibaba Cloud.

Abstract: Multi-cloud strategies are increasingly adopted by modern enterprises to improve agility and resilience and to reduce vendor lock-in. Integrating workloads across providers, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Alibaba Cloud, remains challenging due to interoperability and migration issues. This paper presents a comparative analysis of AWS and Alibaba Cloud, focusing on architectural, service, and policy differences affecting workload migration. Using both provider-native and open source Infrastructure-as-Code tools, we conduct an exploratory case study about the migration of Internet of Things (IoT) workloads. The results highlight key technical trade-offs and best practices for secure multi-cloud deployments, offering guidance for organizations pursuing AWS and Alibaba Cloud interoperability.

</details>


### [362] [Efficient Domain Decomposition for the Helmholtz Equation on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21695)
*Amit Rotem*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents a novel approach for solving the Helmholtz equation using a block-level domain decomposition scheme and a specialized solver, WaveHoltz, optimized for GPU execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to improve the efficiency of solving the Helmholtz equation on modern GPUs, addressing the challenges posed by its indefinite nature and the limitations of existing iterative methods.

Method: The authors introduce a block-level domain decomposition where subdomains are processed concurrently in a single kernel launch, employing WaveHoltz as a solver, which suits GPU architecture due to its low memory usage and lack of reduction operations.

Result: The CUDA implementation on an NVIDIA A100 demonstrates that WaveHoltz achieves 2x-25x speedup compared to MINRES, with performance improvements increasing with subdomain size.

Conclusion: Using single precision for the subdomain solver provides an additional 2x-10x speedup, a significant advantage not achievable by MINRES due to inherent limitations.

Abstract: The Helmholtz equation governs wave propagation in acoustics, electromagnetics, and seismology, but its indefinite nature makes it difficult to solve with iterative methods. Domain decomposition methods are a natural fit for massively parallel architectures, yet mapping efficient Helmholtz solvers onto modern GPUs remains a challenge. We address both with two key contributions: (1) a block-level domain decomposition scheme, in which each subdomain is assigned to a single thread block and all solves run concurrently in a single kernel launch, and (2) WaveHoltz as the subdomain solver. WaveHoltz is a fixed-point iteration that is uniquely well-suited to the GPU execution model due to its minimal memory footprint and no reduction operations. Together, these eliminate device-level synchronizations and replace global memory traffic with shared memory and register-level operations, keeping subdomain data largely resident in L1 and L2 cache. We explore two threading strategies: one degree of freedom per thread for small subdomains, and multiple degrees of freedom per thread for larger ones. Benchmarks of our CUDA based implementation on a NVIDIA A100 show that WaveHoltz achieves 2x-25x speedup over MINRES, with the advantage growing with subdomain size. Crucially, evaluating the subdomain solver in single rather than double precision yields an additional 2x-10x speedup--a benefit largely unattainable by MINRES due to loss of Krylov vector orthogonality under reduced precision.

</details>


### [363] [BatchGen: An Architecture for Scalable and Efficient Batch Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21712)
*Tairan Xu,Leyang Xue,Zhan Lu,Jinfu Deng,Hongyang Xiao,Yinsicheng Jiang,Congjie He,Matej Sandor,Le Xu,Luo Mai*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: BatchGen introduces a sequence coroutine compute model for efficient batch inference on AI computation, significantly improving throughput and reducing completion time on GPU clusters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current inference engines are inadequate for handling large batch workloads due to their reliance on interactive serving execution models, leading to underutilization and inefficiency.

Method: The sequence coroutine compute model treats each sequence as an event-driven coroutine, allowing dynamic workload management and resource reallocation across GPUs.

Result: BatchGen optimizes batch completion time by up to 2.3 times on a 128-GPU cluster and achieves up to 9.6 times better performance compared to leading offloading methods on memory-constrained GPUs.

Conclusion: BatchGen provides a powerful and scalable solution for batch inference, promising better utilization and performance across diverse compute environments.

Abstract: Batch inference has become a central mode of AI computation, yet existing inference engines still rely on execution models designed for interactive serving. When scaled to millions of sequences, batch workloads reveal two fundamental requirements: the ability to handle extreme inter- and intra-sequence load variation that emerges only at runtime, and the ability to sustain high utilization across large fleets of GPUs. Existing systems fail to meet these requirements, losing substantial fractions of achievable throughput.
  We introduce a new architectural foundation for batch inference: the sequence coroutine compute model, which represents each sequence as a fine-grained, event-driven coroutine. This model exposes expressive primitives that allow the runtime to reorganize work dynamically, enabling larger expert-level batches, mitigating stragglers, reallocating work across devices, and maintaining utilization even on cost-effective or memory-constrained GPUs. Building on this abstraction, we implement BatchGen, a production-ready system that uses the coroutine model at cluster scale. On a 128-GPU cluster, BatchGen reduces batch completion time by up to $2.3\times$, and on memory-constrained accelerators it outperforms the strongest offloading baseline by up to $9.6\times$. We will open-source BatchGen at https://github.com/batchgen-project/batchgen

</details>


### [364] [Rethinking Burst Buffer Optimization: Enabling Layout Heterogeneity via Hybrid Analysis and LLM Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21852)
*Yuhan Cai,Huijun Wu,Zhuo Tang,Kehua Guo,Wenzhe Zhang,Zhenwei Wu,Zhouyang Jia,Ruibo Wang,Yong Dong*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Proteus is a semantic-aware burst buffer system that optimizes data layout to align with application I/O patterns, achieving significant performance gains without extensive training or profiling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address performance degradation in burst buffer file systems caused by mismatched data layouts and application I/O patterns in high-performance computing (HPC) systems.

Method: Proteus utilizes a combination of static code structures and lightweight runtime signals to reconstruct application I/O intent and determine optimal data layouts in real time, bypassing the need for extensive training or profiling.

Result: Proteus demonstrates 91.30% decision accuracy and provides up to 3.24x speedup for write-intensive workloads and 2.9x for metadata-intensive workloads in evaluations with HPC applications.

Conclusion: The approach effectively bridges the gap between application behaviors and data organization, enhancing performance and reducing overhead in HPC environments.

Abstract: Burst buffers (BBs) are essential for mitigating I/O bottlenecks in modern HPC systems. However, existing BB file systems often suffer from structural performance degradation due to fixed data layouts that fail to align with diverse application behaviors. While current machine-learning-based optimizations focus primarily on tuning storage stack parameters for a given layout, they offer diminishing returns when a fundamental mismatch exists between I/O patterns and the underlying data organization. Furthermore, these approaches typically incur prohibitive costs due to extensive training or intrusive profiling. To bridge this gap, we present Proteus, a semantic-aware BB system that treats data layout as a first-class optimization dimension. The core insight of Proteus is that application I/O intent can be reconstructed by synergetically combining static code structures with lightweight runtime signals. Through a hybrid pipeline and a single execution probe, Proteus extracts latent semantic cues to determine the optimal layout prior to production runs-eliminating the need for prior training or exhaustive profiling. Evaluation with representative HPC workloads shows that Proteus achieves 91.30\% decision accuracy, delivering up to 3.24$\times$ and 2.9$\times$ speedups for write-intensive and metadata-intensive workloads, respectively.

</details>


### [365] [StickyInvoc: Rethinking Task Models for High-throughput Workflows in the LLM Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22175)
*Thanh Son Phung,Douglas Thain*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents StickyInvoc, a new task model for high-throughput workflows that significantly reduces overhead in LLM inference by maintaining persistent computational states, resulting in a 3.6x speedup in processing time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the performance barriers in high-throughput workflows for LLMs caused by costly state creation and destruction processes.

Method: The paper introduces StickyInvoc, which consists of 'sticky' tasks that create persistent states and 'invocation' tasks that execute computations without recreating states.

Result: The adoption of StickyInvoc in a claim verification workflow led to a 3.6x speedup, enabling 150,000 inferences to be completed in 784 seconds using 186 GPUs.

Conclusion: StickyInvoc effectively decouples state management from computation, greatly enhancing efficiency in high-throughput LLM inference tasks.

Abstract: The integration of LLMs into high-throughput workflows is creating a new class of workloads on HPC clusters that promises to accelerate advances in scientific discovery with unprecedented generative capabilities. However, the traditional task model imposes a prohibitive overhead in this new domain: each task must create its computational state from scratch and destroy it upon completion. For each LLM inference task, this "create-destroy" model forces the repeated and costly transfer of multi-gigabyte model parameters from a long-term, reliable storage to a compute node's local disk, its CPU memory, and finally its GPU memory. This overhead, compounded by the inherently high startup cost of LLM inference, the typical scale of thousands of tasks in high-throughput workflows, and the heterogeneous and preemptible nature of high-throughput resources, presents a significant performance barrier.
  To overcome this barrier, this paper presents StickyInvoc: a symbiotic relationship between two new task models for high-throughput workflows. Specifically, a "sticky" task creates a persistent state on a compute node from a user-provided template, but doesn't execute any goodput computation by itself. Instead, this state is then inherited by subsequent "invocation" tasks, which perform the actual computation without incurring the state creation overhead or destroying the state upon exit. StickyInvoc thus allows the decoupling of the creation and destruction of computational states, allowing the computational state of LLM models to be created once per sticky task and its cost amortized over many subsequent invocation tasks. Our evaluation shows that when rewritten in the StickyInvoc paradigm, a claim verification workflow consisting of 150k inferences achieves a 3.6x speedup on a stable testbed with 20 GPUs, and completes in just 784 seconds by incrementally scaling out to 186 otherwise idle GPUs.

</details>


### [366] [FeLoG: Scalable and Efficient Distributed Graph Embedding with Feedback Loop Mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22180)
*Peng Fang,Arijit Khan,Ziqiang Wu,Zhenli Li,Yibo Zhou,Fang Wang,Dan Feng*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: FeLoG is a system designed for scalable distributed graph embedding, enhancing efficiency through feedback-driven sampling, activity-aware communication, and a round-interleaved pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind FeLoG is to improve the scalability and efficiency of graph embedding as graphs increase in size, addressing issues related to decoupled sampling and training that lead to redundant exploration and low resource utilization.

Method: FeLoG utilizes a feedback-coupled sampling and training approach, prioritizes undertrained nodes, employs activity-aware communication to reduce traffic, and implements a round-interleaved pipeline to enhance CPU-GPU utilization.

Result: FeLoG demonstrated a significant performance improvement with a 27.9x speedup over existing methods, over 53.1% reduction in communication costs, and maintained over 80% CPU-GPU utilization in experiments with large-scale graphs.

Conclusion: The results confirm that FeLoG provides a scalable and efficient solution for distributed graph embedding, effectively addressing critical challenges in the current landscape.

Abstract: Graph embedding maps graph nodes into low-dimensional vectors to support applications such as recommendation, fraud detection, and graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). As graphs scale to billions of edges, scalable and efficient graph embedding has become increasingly important. Existing frameworks commonly adopt a sampling-training paradigm, in which mini-batches are constructed by sampling nodes and their neighbors. However, sampling is typically decoupled from evolving embedding quality, causing redundant exploration of well-trained regions while under-sampling undertrained nodes. At the system level, such decoupling further leads to excessive communication, serialized execution, and low resource utilization in distributed environments. We present FeLoG, a feedback loop-driven system for scalable distributed graph embedding. (1) FeLoG introduces feedback-coupled sampling and training, dynamically prioritizing undertrained nodes according to real-time embedding-quality feedback, thereby reducing redundant computation and accelerating convergence. (2) It employs activity-aware communication that compresses frequently occurring node sequences to reduce intra-machine PCIe traffic and selectively synchronizes frequently updated embeddings to reduce inter-machine communication. (3) It adopts a round-interleaved pipeline that overlaps next-round sampling with current-round training to improve CPU-GPU utilization. Experiments against six state-of-the-art baselines on large-scale graphs show that FeLoG achieves an average speedup of 27.9x, reduces communication cost by more than 53.1%, and sustains over 80% CPU-GPU utilization.

</details>


### [367] [Hardwired Pattern Formation by Mobile Robots with Common Unit Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22386)
*Yuta Kojima,Sébastien Tixeuil,Yukiko Yamauchi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper introduces the hardwired pattern formation (HwPTF) problem, focusing on mobile robots forming a target pattern of specified size, and discusses conditions under which different robot types can solve the problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore new constraints in the pattern formation problem, specifically requiring robots to form a target pattern without the freedom of translation, rotation, and scaling.

Method: The paper evaluates the capabilities of two types of robots: oblivious semi-synchronous and oblivious asynchronous robots, in solving the HwPTF problem under various conditions.

Result: It is shown that two oblivious semi-synchronous robots cannot solve the HwPTF problem with multiplicity two, but they can solve it without multiplicity. Additionally, it is demonstrated that two oblivious asynchronous robots with lights can solve the HwPTF problem, while those without lights cannot.

Conclusion: The paper concludes with the introduction of a size-adjusting algorithm for more than four oblivious semi-synchronous robots, which, when integrated with existing algorithms, provides a solution to the HwPTF problem.

Abstract: The pattern formation (PTF) problem requires mobile robots to form a specified target pattern. Existing papers investigated the PTF problem and revealed the effect of obliviousness and synchronization on distributed coordination of mobile robots. However, the PTF problem allows translation, rotation, and scaling of the target pattern. In this paper, we introduce a novel pattern formation problem, called the hardwired pattern formation (HwPTF) problem that requires the robots to form a given target pattern in a specified size. Although two oblivious semi-synchronous robots cannot solve the HwPTF problem of multiplicity two (i.e., the rendezvous problem), we show that they can solve the HwPTF problem without multiplicity. We also show that two oblivious asynchronous robots equipped with lights can solve the HwPTF problem, while oblivious asynchronous robots cannot. We finally present a size-adjusting algorithm for more than four oblivious semi-synchronous robots, that yields a HwPTF algorithm when combined with some existing pattern formation algorithms.

</details>


### [368] [ASAP: A Disaggregated and Asynchronous Inference System for MoE Prefill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22541)
*Weiwei Chen,Shuang Chen,Lele Li,Qiang Hu,Han Li,Xin Ye,Ming Yan,Zhibin Yu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: ASAP is an asynchronous inference system for Mixture-of-Experts models that improves throughput by 90% by eliminating global synchronization barriers during the prefill phase.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address synchronization stalls in current Mixture-of-Experts model serving due to Data Parallelism and Expert Parallelism, which degrade performance in online servicing.

Method: ASAP disaggregates attention and MoE stages, employing a fully asynchronous execution pipeline with specialized communication primitives and optimizations in request scheduling and model execution.

Result: ASAP is implemented on CloudMatrix384 super-nodes and shown to enhance SLO-compliant prefill throughput by 90% over existing synchronous solutions.

Conclusion: The proposed method significantly enhances the efficiency of MoE model prefill phases, reducing stalls and improving overall performance.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the de facto standard for scaling large language models. To maintain computational efficiency, modern MoE serving systems typically employ a hybrid parallelism strategy, combining Data Parallelism (DP) for attention stages with Expert Parallelism (EP) for MoE stages. However, this design necessitates frequent global synchronization barriers between attention DP groups and experts. In online serving, significant variance in request arrival rates and sequence lengths inherently leads to DP imbalance, causing severe synchronization stalls that degrade Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and system throughput. We present ASAP, an asynchronous inference system specifically designed to accelerate the prefill phase of MoE models. ASAP disaggregates the attention and MoE stages and implements a fully asynchronous execution pipeline. This is achieved through a suite of specialized asynchronous communication primitives and four coordinated optimizations across request scheduling and model execution, which collectively dismantle global synchronization barriers. We implement and evaluate ASAP on CloudMatrix384 super-nodes, demonstrating that it improves SLO-compliant prefill throughput by 90% compared to state-of-the-art synchronous serving solutions.

</details>


### [369] [EchoFlow: A Workload-Aware Parameter Tuning Method for Blockchain Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22934)
*Ben Lian,Linpeng Jia,Xing Chen,Xiaofeng Chen,Yi Sun*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: EchoFlow is a blockchain parameter tuning framework that uses reinforcement learning and a genetic algorithm to optimize performance based on workload characteristics, outperforming existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to optimize blockchain performance by adjusting tunable parameters for varying workloads, as current practices often neglect this adaptability.

Method: EchoFlow implements a distributed reinforcement learning strategy with parallel sampling and incorporates a genetic algorithm for initial sample generation to enhance training efficiency and performance.

Result: Extensive evaluations show that EchoFlow outperforms existing tuning methods and reduces training time across various workload scenarios.

Conclusion: EchoFlow effectively enhances blockchain system performance through adaptive tuning and demonstrates significant practical benefits.

Abstract: Blockchain systems expose a large number of tunable parameters that significantly influence system performance. However, in practice, a single parameter configuration is often applied across different workloads, leaving substantial unexploited performance potential. To address this, we propose EchoFlow, a blockchain parameter tuning framework that adaptively adjusts parameter configurations based on workload characteristics, enabling continuous performance optimization. EchoFlow employs a distributed reinforcement learning approach in which multiple actors perform parallel sampling to mitigate the substantial time required for sample generation in blockchain environments. To further accelerate convergence, we introduce a genetic algorithm during the initial phase of training to generate high-quality samples. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that EchoFlow consistently outperforms existing methods across diverse workload scenarios while also reducing training time, highlighting its effectiveness and practical value.

</details>


### [370] [Decentralized Operations of Decarbonized Chemical Plants with Renewable-driven Transmission Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22973)
*Richard Reed,kazi Arman Ahmed,Saba Ghasemi,Zheyu Jiang,Paritosh Ramanan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper presents a decentralized framework for optimizing electrified ethane cracking operations while addressing data privacy concerns in collaboration with power grid operators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for decarbonization in industrial processes through the electrification of ethane cracking, leveraging renewable energy, and overcoming operational data confidentiality challenges.

Method: A privacy-friendly decentralized framework is proposed, utilizing data isolation and the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, to jointly optimize Unit Commitment and microgrid scheduling problems.

Result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework yields small optimality gaps in joint power and chemical system decisions, with emissions impacts that vary with load.

Conclusion: The study affirms the viability of data isolation in enhancing operational coordination between decarbonized power grids and chemical plants, despite the confidentiality of sensitive operational data.

Abstract: Electrification of ethane cracking offers a promising pathway to industrial decarbonization, provided that the electricity is sourced from renewable energy. However, integrating electrified chemical plant microgrids with a decarbonized power grid requires joint operations planning between Independent System Operators and chemical plants, which is hindered by the highly confidential nature of plant operational data. In this paper, we propose a privacy-friendly decentralized framework based on data isolation that jointly optimizes the Unit Commitment problem in the power system and microgrid scheduling in electrified ethane cracker plants. The framework employs the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, augmented with an auxiliary system-level penalty that accelerates convergence, allowing each subsystem to solve its local subproblem and share only minimal coordination signals. To reflect real-world conditions, numerical experiments are conducted on the ACTIVSg2000 test case, a synthetic model of the Texas transmission network, with 26 chemical plants identified from Texas mapped to their nearest grid connection points. In doing so, we characterize the cost of privacy-friendly decomposition on joint power and chemical system decisions, showing that data isolation results in consistently small optimality gaps, and that its emissions consequences are load-dependent and non-monotone.

</details>


### [371] [LiveServe: Interaction-Aware Serving for Real-Time Omni-Modal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22983)
*Xiangyu Zhi,Peiqi Yin,Sheng Guan,Chenguang Zheng,James Cheng,Xiao Yan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: LiveServe enhances realtime interaction in omni-modal language models (LMs) by optimizing audio playback, scheduling, and key-value (KV) state management for efficient processing and improved response times.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for efficient and responsive speech-centric conversations in omni-modal language models, addressing limitations in existing LLM scheduling and KV offloading that affect user experience.

Method: LiveServe integrates playback progress, speech activity, and barge-in events into the serving pipeline. It prioritizes audio rendering and session management, while employing next-use-aware eviction for KV states to minimize latency.

Result: LiveServe achieves significant improvements in audio time-to-first-play (TTFP), averaging a reduction of 1.55x and up to 2.21x, along with an increase in request throughput by 1.15x on average and 1.56x at peak, while offloading KV reload tasks from critical processing paths.

Conclusion: The proposed LiveServe system demonstrates substantial enhancements in real-time serving capabilities for omni-modal LMs, providing a more efficient interaction experience by managing audio playback and KV state effectively.

Abstract: Realtime omni-modal LMs support speech-centric conversations where users stream inputs, hear generated audio, and interrupt freely. Existing Omni-LM serving systems still rely on throughput-oriented LLM scheduling and LRU KV offloading. These policies ignore audio playback and multi-turn reuse: they may generate tokens far beyond what users hear, wasting work after barge-in, and evict KV state needed in the next turn. LiveServe is an interaction-aware serving system for realtime Omni-LM interaction. It exposes playback progress, speech activity, and barge-in events to the serving pipeline. The scheduler prioritizes first-audio and near-underrun sessions while limiting generation beyond the playback frontier. The KV manager uses next-use-aware eviction and preloads likely-needed KV during user speech to hide reload latency. On vLLM-Omni, LiveServe improves realtime serving across two Omni-LMs and mixed workloads. It lowers P90 audio TTFP by $1.55\times$ on average and up to $2.21\times$, while improving completed-request throughput by $1.15\times$ on average and up to $1.56\times$, and moves most KV reload work off the next-turn critical path.

</details>


### [372] [Nautilus: A Verifiable Hierarchical Federated Learning Framework for Vehicular-Edge-Cloud Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23017)
*Linyang Wu,Linpeng Jia,Hanwen Zhang,Tiantian Duan,Yi Sun*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents Nautilus, a federated learning framework for IoV that improves efficiency and trust via resource-aware scheduling and Zero-Knowledge Proofs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The extreme heterogeneity of vehicular-edge-cloud resources limits efficiency in federated learning for IoV, and dynamic scheduling raises trust concerns.

Method: Nautilus employs a multi-dimensional resource-aware scheduling algorithm combined with a Zero-Knowledge Proof mechanism to enhance scheduling fairness and client compliance.

Result: Experimental results indicate reduced communication overhead and accelerated model convergence while ensuring system integrity.

Conclusion: Nautilus effectively addresses efficiency and trust issues in federated learning for IoV scenarios.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative learning for Internet of Vehicles (IoV) scenarios, but the extreme heterogeneity of vehicular-edge-cloud resources severely limits system efficiency. While dynamic scheduling strategies can mitigate this issue, they introduce new trust concerns: how to verify that scheduling decisions are fair, and whether clients faithfully execute optimization instructions without disclosing private data? This paper proposes Nautilus, a verifiable and efficient federated learning framework. First, we design a multi-dimensional resource-aware scheduling algorithm that dynamically allocates compression ratios and training tasks based on vehicles bandwidth, latency, and computing power, significantly improving system training efficiency. Second, to address the trust deficit in the scheduling process, we introduce a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) mechanism that ensures the fairness of scheduling strategy generation and the compliance of client execution while preserving privacy. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework effectively reduces communication overhead and accelerates model convergence while maintaining system integrity.

</details>


### [373] [Solving Approximate Agreement on continuous and discrete spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23260)
*Augustin Albert,Sergio Rajsbaum*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper examines the wait-free solvability of approximate agreement among $n$ asynchronous processes with crash failures. It defines conditions for validity in various input spaces and proves results for CUB spaces and simplicial complexes regarding the solvability of agreement problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to understand how asynchronous processes can achieve consensus on outputs that are close to each other, despite possible crashes, and identifies the conditions under which this is achievable.

Method: The paper analyzes various metrics and validity conditions for input spaces such as graphs and simplicial complexes, establishing solvability criteria based on the processes' connectivity and dimensionality.

Result: The authors demonstrate that $ε$-agreement is solvable in every CUB space and that simplex agreement in a simplicial complex is solvable for $n+1$ processes if and only if the complex is $(n-1)$-connected.

Conclusion: This work extends previous understanding of approximate agreement in computational models and proves a conjecture related to simplicial complexes, highlighting the significance of connectivity in solving these problems.

Abstract: We consider $n$ asynchronous processes prone to crashes, communicating via shared read-write registers, and study the wait-free solvability of approximate agreement: given inputs, processes must output values that are close to each other, and satisfy a validity property. At the very least, if inputs are identical, all outputs must equal that input.
  The problem has been studied for various input spaces: continuous, discrete, one-dimensional or multidimensional. For metric spaces, validity requires outputs to lie in the convex hull of the inputs. For graphs, and more generally simplicial complexes, several conditions exist. We focus on simplex validity: if inputs span a simplex $σ$, then outputs are in $σ$. Agreement requires that outputs span a simplex.
  Solvability depends on the input space, validity condition, and number of processes. For example, the problem is solvable for all $n$ in the plane, but only for $n \leq 2$ when removing a point. For a graph, solvability for $n=2$ holds iff the graph is connected, but $n\geq 3$ requires acyclicity.
  In the continuous setting, we consider CUB spaces: a broad class of metric spaces admitting a unique convexity definition, subsuming classical $ε$-agreement on $[0,1]$ and $m$-dimensional approximate agreement. Our results show that $ε$-agreement is solvable in every CUB space. In the discrete case, we prove that simplex agreement on a simplicial complex $\mathcal{C}$ is solvable for $n+1$ processes iff $\mathcal{C}$ is $(n-1)$-connected. We discuss several consequences, including a proof of a conjecture by Ledent.

</details>


### [374] [Node-Level Performance and Energy Characterization of Flagship Science Applications on SuperMUC-NG Phase 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23265)
*Salvatore Cielo,Elmira Birang,Alexander Pöppl,Sajad Azizi,Plamen Dobrev,Margarita Egelhofer,Ivan Pribec,Gerald Mathias*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper evaluates the performance and energy efficiency of five scientific workloads on the SuperMUC-NG supercomputer, comparing CPU-only and CPU+GPU configurations. Results show significant improvements in throughput and energy efficiency with GPU offload, although gains depend on problem granularity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to characterize the performance and energy efficiency of high-profile scientific workloads on a leading supercomputing system, addressing the impact of different hardware configurations on computational performance.

Method: Throughput and energy efficiency were measured for five workloads using CPU-only and combined CPU+GPU configurations. Lightweight instrumentation tools were used to gather energy data, and performance comparisons were made based on compute-elements per wall-clock second and per Joule of energy consumed.

Result: GPU offload provides $4-12×$ higher throughput and up to $15×$ better energy efficiency compared to CPU-only execution, with workload dependencies observed particularly in lammps and AthenaK, indicating gains are sensitive to problem granularity.

Conclusion: While GPU use enhances throughput and energy performance, the sensitivity to problem size and the underutilization of CPU power budgets highlight critical considerations in deploying hybrid computing approaches.

Abstract: We present a systematic performance and energy-efficiency characterization of five flagship scientific workloads on SuperMUC-NG phase 2, the 28 PetaFLOPs system at the Leibniz Supercomputing Center (LRZ) equipped with Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ and Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (Ponte Vecchio, PVC) accelerators. The selected codes span molecular dynamics (gromacs, lammps), astrophysics and cosmology (OpenGadget3, AthenaK), and finite-element PDE solvers from the dealii-X Center of Excellence. For each code we measure throughput and energy efficiency expressed as compute-elements per wall-clock second (or per Joule of consumed energy) on a single compute node, comparing CPU-only (SPR) against combined CPU+GPU (SPR+PVC) configurations where available. Energy measurements rely on lightweight code instrumentation with p3em, or the Energy Aware Runtime (EAR) present on the system. Our results show that GPU offload yields $4-12\times$ higher throughput and up to $15\times$ better energy efficiency compared to CPU-only execution, with lammps and AthenaK benefiting most. However, both throughput and energy gains are sensitive to problem granularity: insufficient work per GPU tile erodes the accelerator advantage, as clearly observed in AthenaK at small mesh-block sizes. The power-budget utilization is systematically lower for CPUs than it is for GPUs, indicating that even at peak useful-work rate, most applications running on CPUs leave a significant fraction of the node's thermal envelope unused.

</details>


### [375] [When Staking Rewards Compound: Measuring the Impact of Ethereum's Pectra Upgrade](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23337)
*Mohammed Benseddik,Benjamin Kraner,Claudio J. Tessone*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper analyzes the impact of the 0x02 compounding validators upgrade on Ethereum's beacon chain, highlighting how it affects consensus-layer rewards and stakeholder migration patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the effects of the Pectra upgrade on validator behavior and reward optimization following the increased staking limit.

Method: The authors conducted simulations to evaluate APR uplifts from compounding for different staker types and performed empirical analysis of all active validators to assess adoption and operational barriers.

Result: Compounding yields a +5% relative consensus-layer APR uplift for small stakers, decreasing to under 1% for larger providers, with 0x02 validators recording slightly better median APR.

Conclusion: Migration to 0x02 validators will likely be slow due to operational barriers and lack of incentive improvements, despite the potential network efficiency gains.

Abstract: Ethereum's beacon chain hosts over 920,000 active validators, a number inflated by the legacy 32 ETH stake cap. The Pectra upgrade (May 2025) addresses this by introducing 0x02 compounding validators, raising the maximum stake per validator from 32 to 2,048 ETH and enabling automatic reward reinvestment. This paper examines how compounding affects consensus-layer rewards, whether higher balances provide execution-layer advantages, and whether the APR uplift justifies migration for different staker types. We analyse adoption patterns across solo stakers and staking providers, investigate the role of consolidation (merging multiple 32 ETH validators into one) in early migration, and identify barriers slowing the transition. Through simulation, we find that compounding provides roughly +5% relative consensus-layer APR uplift for small balances, diminishing to under 1% for large staking providers. Empirical analysis of all active beacon chain validators shows 0x02 validators achieving modestly higher median CL APR. Solo stakers show higher relative adoption but face operational barriers, whilst providers cite infrastructure costs and protocol constraints. The results suggest that without improved reward accessibility and stronger economic incentives, 0x02 migration will remain gradual despite its network efficiency benefits.

</details>


### [376] [Development and Design of FLKit: A Structured Onboarding Toolkit for Federated Learning in Health and Life Sciences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23500)
*Ashkan Pirmani,Ilse Vermeulen,Goran Vinterhalter,Lotte Geys,Axel Faes,Muhammad Quamber Ali,Nishkala Sattanathan,Geert Vandeweyer,Yves Moreau,Liesbet M. Peeters*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: FLKit is an onboarding toolkit for federated learning designed for multidisciplinary teams in health and life sciences, providing structured guidance and resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the practical barriers faced by teams starting federated learning projects in the context of strict privacy regulations.

Method: Development of an open, community-maintained toolkit that supports teams through the federated learning lifecycle with role-specific entry points and resources.

Result: FLKit has expanded to 39 pages and includes seven documented projects in various health fields, offering a comprehensive resource directory.

Conclusion: FLKit facilitates collaboration in federated learning for diverse stakeholders in health and life sciences, ensuring accessibility and structured guidance.

Abstract: Federated learning lets institutions train shared models without moving their data, which makes it a natural fit for health and life sciences research under strict privacy regulation. The methods are maturing fast, but the practical barrier now comes earlier: a team starting a federated project meets a scattered mix of frameworks, governance obligations, and unfamiliar roles, with no structured place to begin that fits its own background. FLKit closes that gap. It is an open, community-maintained onboarding toolkit that takes a multidisciplinary team through the full federated learning lifecycle and gives every contributor, clinical, legal, governance, or technical, a role-aware entry point instead of assuming fluency across all four. We modeled it on the ELIXIR Research Data Management Kit and built it with a multidisciplinary core team, a wider consortium supplying milestone reviews and roadmap direction, and external practitioners interviewed to keep the content grounded in real practice. FLKit sits on four lifecycle stages, Governance, Infrastructure, Wrangling, and Analysis, and connects them through 11 role-specific entry points, a cross-disciplinary glossary, a reusable FAIR-aligned FL Story template for planning and documenting projects, and a curated directory of tools, frameworks, and communities. Since the December 2024 demo it has grown to 39 pages across eight sections, with seven FL Stories documenting completed and ongoing projects in multiple sclerosis disability prediction, inflammatory bowel disease, genomics, and brain-computer interfaces. It is openly available at https://uhasselt-biomedicaldatasciences.github.io/federated-learning-toolkit/ and welcomes contributions from across the life sciences.

</details>


### [377] [Concordia: JIT-Compiled Persistent-Kernel Checkpointing for Fault-Tolerant LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23521)
*Yuhang Gan,Yiwei Yang,Yuyi Li,Xiangyu Gao,Yichen Wang,Rain Jiang,Xiaoning Ding,Andi Quinn,Chen Qian*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The paper presents Concordia, a fault-tolerant runtime for large language model (LLM) inference that utilizes GPU-resident execution contexts to preserve state and enable efficient recovery after failures, avoiding the need for extensive application-specific checkpointing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-running LLM agents lose valuable processing state after failure, leading to significant work loss. Existing recovery methods are limited and often inefficient, requiring complete restarts or application-specific logic.

Method: Concordia implements a persistent kernel on GPUs that supports device-level checkpoint hooks, integrates with existing frameworks and libraries, and JIT-compiles specialized handlers for various LLM states to facilitate efficient recovery.

Result: Concordia enables a lock-free, always-on executor to manage compute and recovery tasks, ensuring that state is retained and efficiently recovered without involving the host CPU during critical operations.

Conclusion: The proposed system addresses the limitations of current fault tolerance mechanisms by providing a robust infrastructure for maintaining state within LLM inference workloads, significantly enhancing resilience against GPU and communicator failures.

Abstract: Long-running LLM agents keep valuable state resident on GPUs: KV caches, request schedulers, communication state, and sometimes online adapters. Losing this state after a GPU or communicator failure can discard minutes to hours of work, yet existing recovery mechanisms either restart the whole serving stack or require application-specific checkpoint logic inside every attention and runtime component. This paper argues that fault tolerance for such workloads needs a GPU-resident execution context: checkpoint hooks must run at device synchronization points, observe binary kernels that frameworks and libraries actually execute, and recover without putting the host CPU on the critical path.
  We present Concordia, a runtime that uses a device-resident persistent kernel as the substrate for fault-tolerant LLM inference. Concordia interposes on GPU module loading and supports PTX- and SASS-level instrumentation, allowing checkpoint and pause hooks to be inserted below framework code and library boundaries. For each registered LLM state region, Concordia JIT-compiles a specialized delta-checkpoint handler -- for example, a KV-block scanner, adapter-page scanner, or recovery applier -- and hot-swaps it into the persistent kernel's operator table. The persistent kernel consumes a lock-free ring buffer of compute, checkpoint, append-log, and recovery tasks, so the same always-on executor triggers dirty-page detection, stages deltas, and appends committed records to a CPU-visible log in CXL memory or host DRAM.

</details>


### [378] [Kamera: Unified Position-Invariant Multimodal KV Cache for Training-Free Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23581)
*Bole Ma,Jan Eitzinger,Harald Koestler,Gerhard Wellein*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper proposes a method to enhance efficiency in multimodal agents by addressing the limitations of naive key-value (KV) reuse during video frame and UI screenshot processing. By introducing a low-rank conditioning patch, the authors enable effective cross-chunk binding without recomputation, optimizing performance in multimodal tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the inefficiencies observed in multimodal agents that repeatedly re-encode video frames and UI screenshots. Traditional KV reuse lacks the ability to leverage cross-chunk conditioning, leading to reduced multi-hop accuracy.

Method: The authors introduce a low-rank conditioning patch stored alongside each position-free chunk to address the deficiencies of naive KV reuse. This approach allows the reordering, relocation, and recall of cached chunks without requiring extensive recomputation.

Result: The proposed method demonstrates significant improvement in task accuracy on cross-chunk binding benchmarks, specifically in scenarios like MM-NIAH and two-page doc-QA, while maintaining a smaller KV footprint and achieving near exact KV reconstruction in production environments.

Conclusion: The patching solution outperforms previous designs by enhancing both single-hop recall and multi-hop accuracy, particularly in redundant vision and video streams, thereby optimizing resource utilization in multimodal agents.

Abstract: Multimodal agents repeatedly re-examine the same video frames, UI screenshots, and rendered artifacts as their context window slides and reasoning iterates, yet every look-back re-encodes from scratch, because prefix caches serve reuse only at a fixed leading position. We show this recompute is avoidable, and identify exactly what naive KV reuse loses: the cross-chunk conditioning a chunk absorbs from its neighbours. This loss is asymmetric. The direct readout of a cached chunk is recovered exactly and for free by the standard state-merge. What remains is a diffuse, low-rank residue concentrated in deep layers, invisible to single-hop retrieval but precisely what multi-hop reasoning binds on. Blind reuse therefore leaves single-hop recall intact while halving multi-hop accuracy; this is the failure mode prior position-independent caches, designed for single-context or single-image reuse, do not address. We repair it with a small, training-free low-rank conditioning patch stored alongside each position-free chunk. Reuse reduces to one operator across MLA, GQA, and MHA: exact RoPE re-rotation to any target position, plus the patch that restores cross-chunk binding. This makes three window operations cheap: reorder (one patch serves every ordering of a cached set), sliding-window survival (surviving chunks relocate via rotation only, zero re-encode), and recall (an evicted chunk is rehydrated by its patch, never re-encoded). A rank-m patch recovers full task accuracy on cross-chunk-binding benchmarks, MM-NIAH across two attention families and two-page doc-QA, at a fraction of the KV footprint, and reconstructs re-prefill KV to within bf16 rounding in a production SGLang kernel across six backbones. The conditioning signal is strongest in redundant vision and video streams, making our solution most impactful where multimodal agents spend their recompute budget.

</details>


<div id='eess.SP'></div>

# eess.SP [[Back]](#toc)

### [379] [Beamforming and RIS-Aided Ambient Backscatter Communications with Residual-Feature SVM Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20741)
*Aobakwe Makgarapa,Burhan Wafai,Sangarapillai Lambotharan,Mahsa Derakhshani*

Main category: eess.SP

TL;DR: The paper explores the enhancement of ambient backscatter communication (AmBC) reliability using reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) and multi-antenna techniques, demonstrating improved signal quality and reduced error rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the reliability of ambient backscatter communication in obstructed environments by leveraging reconfigurable intelligent surfaces for better signal propagation.

Method: An RIS-aided AmBC system is proposed, utilizing phase alignment for the source-RIS-tag link and beamforming techniques for enhancing signal detection, integrating MMSE equalization and SVM for classification.

Result: Simulation results indicate significant bit-error-rate reductions and highlight that system performance is more dependent on the number of RIS elements than on reader antenna counts, with optimal performance achievable at moderate RIS sizes.

Conclusion: The proposed approach effectively enhances AmBC detection reliability and spectral efficiency while minimizing hardware costs.

Abstract: Ambient backscatter communication (AmBC) enables battery-free connectivity by modulating data onto existing radio-frequency (RF) signals, eliminating the need for dedicated power sources. However, its reliability degrades when direct wireless channels are obstructed or severely faded. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) offer a solution by creating a favorable propagation environment through the control of the phases of incident signals, thereby strengthening wireless links.
  This paper investigates an RIS-aided AmBC system that jointly exploits physical-layer reconfiguration and statistical learning to restore detection reliability under such conditions. The RIS phase profile is aligned for the source-RIS-tag link, while a multi-antenna reader applies receive beamforming to steer toward the RF source and the tag separately. At the reader, a hypothesis-based minimum mean square error (MMSE) equalizer reconstructs the ambient symbol under each candidate tag state and produces a pair of residual features, which are classified by a support vector machine (SVM) with a Gaussian kernel. We make the physical-layer-to-learning coupling explicit, i.e., RIS phase alignment and beamforming improve the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), thereby rendering the residual features more separable and reducing classification error.
  Simulation results show that the proposed RIS-beamforming-SVM detector achieves substantial bit-error-rate (BER) gains over RIS-energy, SVM, and SVM-beamforming baselines across a wide SINR range, that the spectral-efficiency gains are governed more strongly by the number of RIS elements than by the number of reader antennas, and that performance saturates with a moderate RIS size, allowing near-optimal operation at reduced hardware cost.

</details>


### [380] [Velocity Information Geometry of Coherent Intra-CPI Waveform Agility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20907)
*Charles E Thornton*

Main category: eess.SP

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how carrier frequency and bandwidth variations affect radar velocity estimation limits, demonstrating that carrier sequences significantly influence the estimation bound and proposing design principles for effective carrier hopping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap in understanding velocity estimation limits when radars vary carrier frequency and bandwidth in spectrum-sharing environments.

Method: The study employs a resolved-bin slow-time model for coherent agile-CPI processing, deriving the effective Fisher information for radial velocity based on carrier-time sequencing and SNR weighting; it verifies results through Fisher matrix analysis and Monte-Carlo methods.

Result: The paper finds that the correlation between carrier offset and slow time can greatly affect velocity estimation; randomized carrier hops are favorable, whereas ramp-correlated hops can deteriorate performance, while bandwidth sequence does not impact the CRB under matched filtering.

Conclusion: The design principle advises that carrier hopping strategies must ensure not only spectrum sharing but also the preservation of critical velocity-information.

Abstract: Spectrum sharing forces radars to vary carrier frequency and bandwidth on a pulse-to-pulse basis within a coherent processing interval (CPI). While the resulting range-Doppler distortion is well-studied, the corresponding velocity estimation limit is not. We show that in the resolved-bin slow-time model of coherent agile-CPI processing, the effective Fisher information for radial velocity is the SNR-weighted energy of the carrier-time lever arm that survives projection out of the range and phase nuisance subspace. The carrier sequence thus sets the projection geometry, while the bandwidth sequence enters only through SNR weighting. Two consequences follow. First, the carrier sequence inflates the bound by a closed-form factor governed by the correlation between carrier offset and slow time: randomized or orthogonalized hops are nearly harmless, while ramp-correlated hops can severely degrade velocity information. Second, under matched filtering at equal pulse energy, the velocity Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) is invariant to the bandwidth sequence; a corollary recasts the output-SNR loss of agile-CPI mismatched filtering as a processing cost entering only through a per-pulse mismatch loss. The bound is verified against a brute-force Fisher matrix and Monte-Carlo maximum-likelihood estimation. The result yields a design principle: carrier hopping should be chosen not only for spectral coexistence but also to preserve the velocity-information residual.

</details>


### [381] [Asynchronous Multi-Channel USF: Modified CRT for Modulo Unfolding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21012)
*Ruiming Guo,Ayush Bhandari*

Main category: eess.SP

TL;DR: This paper presents an asynchronous multi-channel Unlimited Sampling Framework (MC-USF) that improves reconstruction accuracy by eliminating the need for strict channel synchronization, overcoming challenges of timing mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the limitations of existing MC-USF methods which rely on timing synchronization, thereby making them prone to inaccuracies due to jitter and other timing errors.

Method: An asynchronous MC-USF architecture is introduced, utilizing graph-based signal lifting to enhance reconstruction robustness against temporal misalignment.

Result: Numerical experiments show that the proposed architecture enables accurate signal recovery despite the absence of synchronization, making it more feasible for practical applications.

Conclusion: The introduction of this asynchronous approach leads to improved implementations of multi-channel USF, catering to real-world scenarios where timing precision cannot be guaranteed.

Abstract: The Unlimited Sampling Framework (USF) overcomes the traditional trade-off between dynamic range and digital resolution, achieving performance unattainable with standard ADCs. Its multi-channel extension (MC-USF) enables reconstruction from multiple folded measurements at critical sampling rates. Existing MC-USF methods typically rely on Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)-based unfolding, which requires strict channel-level sampling synchronization and is therefore vulnerable to timing mismatch, jitter, and drift. This paper introduces an asynchronous MC-USF architecture that eliminates the need for synchronization. By viewing spatial-temporal signal lifting as inducing smoothness over a graph of sensing channels, we develop a reconstruction strategy robust to temporal misalignment. Numerical experiments validate the approach, demonstrating accurate recovery and enabling more practical multi-channel USF implementations.

</details>


### [382] [DPD-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Low Complexity Digital Predistortion in 5G Analog Radio-over-Fiber Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21178)
*Bilal Khalid,Fabio Cavaliere,Luca Giorgi,Pedro Freire,Sergei K. Turitsyn,Jaroslaw E. Prilepsky*

Main category: eess.SP

TL;DR: Presentation of a KAN-based DPD model for 5G analog RoF fronthaul, achieving lower EVM compared to other methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve digital predistortion (DPD) performance in 5G systems, focusing on enhancing linearity and reducing error vector magnitude (EVM).

Method: Development of a KAN-based DPD model that was tested against multi-layer perceptron and Volterra-based GMP models.

Result: KAN-based model achieves 24.2% lower EVM than multi-layer perceptron and 29.6% lower than Volterra-based GMP at equivalent Bit Operations.

Conclusion: KAN requires ~52% fewer BOPs than a perceptron to maintain an EVM below 2%, indicating its efficiency for 5G applications.

Abstract: We demonstrate the first KAN-based DPD model for 5G analog RoF fronthaul link, achieving a 24.2% lower EVM than multi-layer perceptron and 29.6% lower than Volterra-based GMP at equivalent Bit Operations. To attain an EVM below 2%, KAN requires ~52% fewer BOPs than a perceptron.

</details>


### [383] [Physics-Informed Neural Optimization Based Antenna Coding Design for Pixel Antenna Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21235)
*Taoning Zhan,Shanpu Shen,Danny H. K. Tsang*

Main category: eess.SP

TL;DR: This paper introduces a new optimization algorithm, PINO, for antenna coding design in pixel antennas, which significantly enhances efficiency and performance compared to traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the NP-hard challenge of antenna coding design and the limitations of conventional heuristic search algorithms in terms of computational complexity.

Method: The proposed PINO algorithm combines a deep convolutional neural network with a Gumbel-Sigmoid continuous relaxation within a differentiable physics engine to reframe the binary optimization problem into a differentiable format suitable for gradient descent methods.
